The Mountain Peacock-Pheasant Polyplectron inopinatum remains one of the least studied galliforms, but recent field observations in the montane forests of the Malay Peninsula have begun to clarify its early life history. Eggs are typically incubated at 37 °C [T = 37 °C], and incubation proceeds for roughly 20 days [ab = roughly 20 days] before pipping begins. Hatchlings emerge at a remarkably modest size, with a neonatal wet body mass of approximately 27 grams [Wwb = approximately 27 grams]. This initial mass is notably low even among polyplectrine pheasants, suggesting that a substantial portion of the yolk reserves must fuel rapid early growth in the cool, humid cloud-forest environment. The chick is semi-precocial, leaving the nest scrape within hours to forage under the hen's close supervision, though the downy young still rely on the female for thermal brooding during the first several nights.

By the third day after hatching, under the thermal conditions the adults typically experience during their active foraging periods (40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]), the flight feathers have begun to emerge and the young bird achieves its first brief, fluttering flights, marking the fledging milestone at just 3 days after hatching [tx = 3 days after hatching]. This extremely rapid fledging interval is among the shortest recorded for any galliform of comparable body size and likely reflects an adaptive response to intense nest predation pressure in the understory. Following fledging, the precocial chick continues to gain mass steadily, and the female leads her brood through dense thickets in search of invertebrates and fallen fruits. The brood remains cohesive for several weeks, with the male sometimes joining the family party after the eggs have hatched, a behavior rarely documented in the genus Polyplectron.

Puberty in Polyplectron inopinatum, albeit poorly documented, is hypothesized to occur at approximately 100 days after hatching [tp = approximately 100 days after hatching] based on extrapolation from a single captive-reared individual maintained at 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. At this stage the subadult birds begin to develop the characteristic ocellated plumage of the genus, and males initiate soft, whirring display calls directed at females. The onset of gonadal maturation appears to be tied to body condition rather than strictly to chronological age; individuals in suboptimal habitats may delay maturity by an additional season. Comparatively, the congeneric Palawan Peacock-Pheasant attains sexual maturity later, though reliable data for that species remain scarce. Further captive breeding efforts are urgently needed to refine this provisional estimate and to confirm its repeatability across different thermal regimes.

First reproduction likely occurs relatively late compared to the onset of puberty, with the first brood of eggs laid approximately 365 days after hatching [tR = approximately 365 days after hatching] when the birds are maintained at 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. This value is drawn from the closely related Polyplectron napoleonis and may serve as a working approximation until species-specific data become available for P. inopinatum. Females construct a shallow nest on the forest floor, lining it with leaves and ferns, and deposit a clutch containing between 16 and 24 eggs [N_R_i = a clutch containing between 16 and 24 eggs]. The annual reproductive output is constrained by the long montane dry season; most broods are initiated at the onset of the rains when insect prey becomes abundant. In a typical year, a female raises only a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], though replacement clutches are possible if the first is lost early in incubation.

Adult body size exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in this species. Females reach an ultimate wet weight of 650 grams [Wwi = 650 grams], whereas males are substantially heavier, attaining an ultimate wet weight of 800 grams [Wwi = 800 grams]. This size disparity is consistent with a polygynous or weakly promiscuous mating system, in which larger males presumably prevail in intrasexual contests for display sites. Maximum longevity has not been directly measured for Polyplectron inopinatum, but based on records from the closely allied Polyplectron napoleonis, a lifespan of 15 years [am = 15 years] at 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C] is considered a reasonable estimate under captive conditions. In the wild, senescence likely sets in earlier owing to predation, disease, and the energetic demands of repeated breeding attempts in a seasonally resource-limited montane habitat.
